lead: AC power has three parts. A sinusoidal voltage and current make instantaneous power pulse twice per cycle. The average of that pulse is active power P; it does useful work or produces heat. Reactive power Q swings energy into and out of inductors and capacitors with no net transfer. Apparent power S is the plain product of RMS voltage and current; it sizes wires, fuses and transformers. Power factor tells what fraction of S becomes P, and utilities charge extra for poor power factor. This chapter defines these quantities and links them in the power triangle.
prereq: You need: RMS values from Chapter 2.1 and impedance phase angle from Chapter 2.4.

blocks.text: Let v(t) = V<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt) and i(t) = I<sub>m</sub> sin(ωt − φ). Instantaneous power is p(t) = v(t)i(t), in watts (W). It changes with time. Its average over one cycle is active power P. For sine waves, P = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>cos φ. V<sub>rms</sub> and I<sub>rms</sub> are RMS values (Chapter 2.1). φ is the angle by which current lags voltage. P is in W. It leaves the source as heat, light, shaft work or battery charging.

Reactive power is Q = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>sin φ, in volt-ampere reactive (var). It is not fake power. An inductor stores energy in its magnetic field; a capacitor stores energy in its electric field. That energy returns to the source each half cycle. Net transfer over a full cycle is zero. Q measures this exchange. Some syllabi call Q reactive volt-amperes.

Apparent power is S = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>, in volt-ampere (VA). It is the product of the voltmeter and ammeter readings, ignoring phase. S sizes cables, fuses, switches and transformer windings, because their limits depend on current and voltage magnitude.

Power factor is PF = cos φ = P/S. It is a pure number from 0 to 1 for normal loads. A pure resistor has φ = 0, PF = 1, P = S, Q = 0. A pure inductor has current lagging by 90°, PF = 0 lagging, P = 0, Q = S. A pure capacitor has current leading by 90°, PF = 0 leading, Q = −S under the lagging-positive convention. Real motors and transformers are inductive: current lags voltage, so PF is lagging. Capacitor banks make current lead and give leading PF.
Current angle = −φ with voltage as reference. An inductor has φ = +90° and current at −90°; a capacitor has φ = −90° and current at +90°.

With voltage as reference, V = V<sub>rms</sub>∠0°. A lagging current is I = I<sub>rms</sub>∠−φ for φ > 0. A leading current has a negative φ. Fix this sign convention before you call Q positive or negative. The formulas use RMS values. Do not mix peak and RMS values: V<sub>m</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>cos φ is √2 times too large, so divide by √2 (multiply by 1/√2). The 1/2 factor applies only when both voltage and current are peak values: P = (V<sub>m</sub>I<sub>m</sub>/2)cos φ.

Complex power is S = P + jQ. Here j is the imaginary unit. The same letter S also means the magnitude: |S| = S = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>. P is the real part in W; Q is the imaginary part in var. The power triangle has |S| as hypotenuse, P adjacent to φ, and Q opposite φ: P = S cos φ, Q = S sin φ, S = √(P² + Q²). The angle of complex S is φ. Lagging loads have Q > 0; leading loads have Q < 0 under the same convention.

The triangle for S = 2300 VA at PF 0.8 lagging has P = 1840 W and Q = 1380 var. The figure shows this split. The cable carries the full 2300 VA, not just 1840 W. A transformer rated 2300 VA can deliver only 1840 W to this load. Raising PF toward 1 raises the useful P available from the same VA rating. Three-phase power uses the same cos φ term; see Chapter 2.7.

figure.caption: Power triangle for the worked example: apparent power 2300 VA splits into active power 1840 W at cos φ and reactive power 1380 var at sin φ. Notice that the two parts add as sides of a right triangle, not as plain numbers.

spec.aria: Power triangle as a tree: apparent power S = 2300 VA splits into active power P = 1840 W along cos φ and reactive power Q = 1380 var along sin φ.

examples.question: A 230 V rms, 50 Hz source supplies a load that draws 10 A rms at 0.8 power factor lagging. (a) Find S, P, the phase angle φ and Q. (b) With V = 230∠0° V rms, write the current phasor. (c) State whether Q is positive or negative under the lagging-positive convention.
steps: Given: V<sub>rms</sub> = 230 V, I<sub>rms</sub> = 10 A, PF = 0.8 lagging.
Active power: P = S cos φ = 2300 × 0.8 = 1840 W.
Phase angle: φ = cos⁻¹(0.8) = 36.87°. Current lags, so its angle is −36.87° with V as reference.
Reactive power: Q = S sin φ = 2300 × 0.6 = 1380 var. Lagging current gives Q = +1380 var.
Current phasor: I = 10∠−36.87° A rms when V = 230∠0° V rms.
examples.answer: S = 2300 VA, P = 1840 W, φ = 36.87°, Q = +1380 var (lagging), and I = 10∠−36.87° A rms with V = 230∠0° V rms.
examples.check:
import math
V = 230
I = 10
pf = 0.8
S = V * I
P = S * pf
phi = math.degrees(math.acos(pf))
Q = S * math.sin(math.acos(pf))
print(S)
print(int(round(P)))
print(round(phi, 2))
print(int(round(Q)))
print(I)
print(-round(phi, 2))

traps: Peak versus RMS: P = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>cos φ. Using peak values gives a result too large by a factor of 2; RMS is the standard for power.
Cos/sin swap: P uses cos φ, Q uses sin φ. At PF 0.8, P is 0.8S, not 0.6S.
Unit slip: P in W, Q in var, S in VA. PF has no unit. Do not write Q in W or S in W.
Sign convention: lagging current is not automatically positive Q. It is positive only if you define Q = V I sin φ with φ positive for lagging. Fix the convention first.
PF angle: PF = 0.8 means φ = cos⁻¹0.8 = 36.87°, not 0.8°. PF is not an angle and not a percentage unless written as 80%.

quiz.q: Define active, reactive and apparent power. Give the unit of each.
quiz.a: Active power P = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>cos φ is average power in W. Reactive power Q = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub>sin φ is in var. Apparent power S = V<sub>rms</sub>I<sub>rms</sub> is in VA.

quiz.q: Why is the average power of a pure inductor zero even though current flows?
quiz.a: Voltage and current are 90° apart. Energy stored in the magnetic field in one quarter cycle returns in the next. The positive and negative p(t) halves cancel over a full cycle, so P = V I cos 90° = 0.

quiz.q: A 120 V rms load draws 5 A rms at 0.6 PF lagging. Find S, P and Q.
Two loads each take 1000 VA at 230 V rms. Load A has PF 1; load B has PF 0.5 lagging. Compare their active power, reactive power and current.
quiz.a: Both draw I = 1000/230 = 4.35 A rms. A: P = 1000 W, Q = 0. B: P = 500 W, φ = 60°, Q = 866 var. Same cable current but B does half the useful work.

quiz.q: Current leads voltage by 30°. Find PF and the sign of Q under the lagging-positive convention.
quiz.a: PF = cos 30° = 0.866 leading. Since current leads, φ = −30° and Q = V I sin(−30°) is negative.

quiz.q: Why do utilities penalize low power factor?
quiz.a: For the same P, low PF needs larger current. That means thicker cables, larger transformers, more I²R loss and more voltage drop. The utility must supply more VA for the same billed W.

quiz.q: A load has P = 800 W and Q = 600 var lagging. Find S and PF.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power factor correction is routine in factories: capacitor banks switch in steps as motors start and stop. Utilities meter reactive energy and apply kVAh or PF penalties. Grid inverters on solar farms can inject or absorb reactive power to support voltage. Search next for static VAR compensator, kVAh tariff, and capacitor sizing for PF correction.
